title: Chords & Harmony

learn.summary: Harmony is intervals stacked into chords, and chords moving in progressions are the engine under every song. A huge share of popular music runs on just four chords from one key. Learn to build triads and hear progressions and you can accompany, write, and decode songs for life.

do: Look up the chords to one song you love and count how many distinct chords it actually uses — most people are shocked it is three or four.

children.title: Triads

learn.summary: A triad stacks two thirds: root, third, fifth. Major = 4 then 3 semitones (C-E-G); minor = 3 then 4 (C-Eb-G); diminished = 3 then 3. That single semitone swap between major and minor is the biggest emotional switch in music.

do: Build C, F, G major and A, D, E minor triads on a piano app — play each and say its notes aloud, twice through.

children.title: The I-V-vi-IV Engine

learn.summary: In C major: C-G-Am-F. This one loop (and its rotation vi-IV-I-V) drives hundreds of hits — Let It Be, Don't Stop Believin', With or Without You. The Roman numerals mean it transposes anywhere: uppercase for major chords, lowercase for minor. Learn it in one key and you have learned it in twelve.

do: Play or hum the C-G-Am-F loop, then sing the chorus of any pop song over it — find two songs this week that fit.

children.title: Hearing Chord Changes

learn.summary: Start by hearing when the chord changes, not which chord it becomes — most pop changes land on bar lines. Then track the bass note: the bassist almost always plays the root. Home-versus-away is the first distinction: the I chord feels settled, everything else feels in motion.

do: Play a simple song and raise your hand every time the chord changes — check your hits against the chord sheet afterward.
